extracted.intended_audience: people preparing or evaluating notice-and-comment administrative rulemaking submissions (advocates, affected individuals, administrative law scholars, agency staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating public comments that advance a 'dignitary' theory of administrative due process — emphasizing recognition, lived experience, and identity-based claims alongside traditional technical or statutory arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission belt (faithful execution of legislative will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithful execution of legislative will — Statutory interpretation; intent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 'transmission belt' theory, comments should provide statutory interpretation and evidence of legislative intent. Such comments are evaluated by how well they explicate and apply the statute or legislative history to the rulemaking question. Use citations to statutory text, legislative history, and authoritative construction to meet this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise (specialist knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialist knowledge — Technical analysis, data, methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments grounded in 'expertise' should supply technical analysis, empirical data, methodological explanation, and citations to studies or technical sources. Scoring favors rigor, replicability, and clear presentation of evidence and methods. Avoid unsubstantiated assertions; include data, sources, and a description of analytical techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignitary theory (recognition of affected persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of affected persons — Lived experience, identity, value claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mashaw's dignitary theory treats participation as constitutive: comments that articulate lived experience and identity have independent normative value even absent technical expertise or statutory citation. Agencies are obligated to recognize affected persons as bearers of dignity; thus these comments should be treated as substantively important. Guidance: present lived experience clearly; do not feel compelled to translate every claim into technical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify as a member of an affected community
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the commenter as a member of an affected community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State plainly who you are and your relation to the regulated activity or population. Self-identification signals standing under the dignitary frame and helps the agency appreciate the source of the lived-experience claim. Include relevant community affiliations, roles, or demographic information that contextualize the perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe human impact in concrete terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the human impact of the rule in concrete terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, particularized descriptions (anecdotes, scenarios, day-to-day effects) of how the rule will affect persons' dignity, autonomy, or social standing. Use concrete examples rather than abstract claims where possible; quantify impacts if feasible. The aim is to convey real-world consequences that illustrate the normative stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate the value at stake (dignity, autonomy, equality, recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate the value at stake — dignity, autonomy, equality, recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which moral or normative value the rule implicates (e.g., dignity, autonomy, equality) and why that value matters in the regulatory context. Tie the normative claim to how the rule will affirm or deny those values for affected persons. This helps agencies and reviewers map lived-experience claims onto broader legal and ethical frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim acknowledgment as the relevant remedy (not merely policy change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim the agency's obligation of acknowledgment, not merely policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Mashaw, a key remedial demand is acknowledgment (responsive engagement), not only adoption of a preferred policy. Frame requests to the agency to acknowledge harms, record perspectives, or explain why it cannot accommodate a dignitary concern, in addition to proposing policy changes. Note that even rejected claims merit substantive, respectful responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative form effectively to communicate lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative form is appropriate for dignitary comments; the comment need not be structured as a legal argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ storytelling techniques (concrete scenes, first-person voice, chronological narrative) to convey lived experience and emotional/relational impacts. Narrative is an acceptable and often effective mode for dignitary claims, but clarity and relevance to the rulemaking question should be maintained. Narrative does not preclude adding brief explanatory linking language to statutory or policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the comment to statutory or regulatory values
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect to a value (autonomy, equality, dignity, fairness) that the statutory framework should respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, show how the dignitary claim relates to values embedded in the statute, regulatory purpose, or constitutional principles. This connection helps integrate identity-based claims into existing administrative decisionmaking even when the primary mode is narrative or testimonial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation caution: preserve dignitary value alongside instrumental criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Mashaw's framework is theoretically rich but operationally indeterminate. Comments grounded in dignity claims are important but harder to evaluate by standard quality criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing rubrics or evaluative processes, avoid reducing dignitary comments to purely instrumental metrics (e.g., data counts, citation counts). Design assessment practices that permit qualitative judgment, recognize acknowledgment as a legitimate agency response, and include procedures for responsive engagement even when the comment does not propose a technical fix. Be explicit about how dignity-based submissions will be considered to prevent marginalization.
